h1:
Ang Thong Temples & Culture
Old Riverside Wats Worth a Stop
intro: Ang Thong is a small province packed with old temples along the Chao Phraya River. Many of them go back to the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya periods, and they hold Buddha images that people from all over central Thailand make a point of coming to pay respects to — a long reclining Buddha, an old gilded reclining figure, and Luang Pho To seated in a tall viharn. We've picked the temples that are genuinely open to visitors, with notes on what to look for, how long to spend, and how to string them into a single-day route.

blocks.html: If you had to sum up Ang Thong for temple lovers in one phrase, it would be "big Buddha images." This province has one of the longest reclining Buddhas in the country, an old reclining figure that was once dragged inland to escape an eroding riverbank, and a Luang Pho To in a viharn first commissioned by Somdej Phra Phutthachan (To Phrommarangsi). Most of the temples cluster along the Chao Phraya and its tributaries, so you can drive from one to the next comfortably in a single day — the gaps between them are usually no more than 20–30 minutes.

blocks.text: The Buddha images people come to pay respects to

blocks.html: These four are the main reason people travel to Ang Thong. Each has its own story and scale. We've ordered them by historical significance and how popular they are with visitors.

items.name: Reclining Buddha, Wat Khun Inthapramun (Pho Thong district)
items.blurb: An open-air reclining Buddha around 50 metres long — one of the longest in Thailand. It's thought to date to the Sukhothai period. The figure originally sat inside a viharn, but the hall burned down and collapsed, leaving the Buddha exposed to sun and rain out in the Pho Thong fields for over a century. Today it has been restored and beautifully gilded, with a wide plaza and a new viharn to walk around.

items.name: Reclining Buddha, Wat Pa Mok Worawihan (Pa Mok district)
items.blurb: A brick-and-stucco reclining Buddha, gilded all over, around 22 metres long, lying on its right side in the lion-rest pose. The head rests on a pillow finely decorated with gold-on-lacquer work. This is a royal temple, and there's a story that during the Ayutthaya period the figure was dragged about 168 metres back from the river to save it from the eroding bank.
items.meta: Open daily ~08:00–17:00 · On the Chao Phraya, Pa Mok district

items.name: Luang Pho To (Phra Maha Phutthaphim), Wat Chaiyo Worawihan (Chaiyo district)
items.blurb: A large seated Buddha in the meditation pose inside a tall viharn, with a lap width of about 16 metres and a height of around 22 metres. It was first commissioned by Somdej Phra Phutthachan (To Phrommarangsi), later rebuilt during the reign of King Rama V and granted a royal name. The tall hall lets light fall on the image beautifully in the mid-morning.
items.meta: Open daily ~08:00–17:00 · On the Chao Phraya, Chaiyo district

items.name: Somdej Phra Si Mueang Thong, Wat Ton Son (Mueang district)
items.blurb: A large cast-metal Buddha in the subduing-Mara pose at Ang Thong's town temple, sitting on the Chao Phraya right in the centre of town. It was built in stages from around 1945 onward. Locals come to pay respects here as the provincial temple, and it's easy to reach since it's right in the town centre.
items.meta: Open daily ~08:00–17:00 · In Ang Thong town centre

blocks.title: Worth knowing before you go
blocks.html: The reclining Buddha at Wat Khun Inthapramun is out in the open, and the midday sun is harsh. Go in the morning or late afternoon for better photos and less heat. At the royal temples like Pa Mok and Chaiyo, dress modestly — no sleeveless tops or shorts inside the viharn.

blocks.text: Riverside temples and Chao Phraya valley culture

blocks.html: The charm of Ang Thong's temples is their relationship with the river. Many old temples face the Chao Phraya, because in the past travel and trade ran mainly along the water, so the temples were both places of worship and the centre of riverbank communities. Some still keep traces of Ayutthaya-era art in their ordination halls and mural paintings.

items: Ayutthaya-style halls and viharns — look at the roof shapes, doorway arches and old stucco work that several temples still preserve.
Murals and gold-on-lacquer work — like the gold-on-lacquer pillow at Wat Pa Mok, fine craftsmanship that's hard to find these days.
Markets and communities by the temple gate — many temples have food and souvenir stalls out front, so after paying respects you can sit down to local snacks.
Seasonal merit festivals — during the Buddhist Lent period and each temple's annual fair things get especially lively, and if your timing lines up you get the full atmosphere.

blocks.text: Other temples and cultural stops worth adding

items.name: Wat Muang (Wiset Chai Chan district)
items.blurb: Home to an enormous subduing-Mara Buddha you can see from far away. Around the temple are stucco scenes depicting heaven and hell — good for photos and making merit.

items.name: Ekkarat drum-making village (Pa Mok district)
items.blurb: An old drum-making community in Ang Thong. Watch the hides being stretched and the wood being turned — a craft that's still made and sold for real.

items.name: Bang Sadet court-doll village (Pa Mok district)
items.blurb: A court-doll workshop set up under a royal-initiative project. Watch the dolls being made and support the handiwork. It's near Wat Pa Mok, so it's easy to combine.

blocks.text: A one-day temple route, linked together

blocks.html: Ang Thong is a great pick for a one-day temple trip from Bangkok, because the main temples aren't far apart. Here's a sample route that flows smoothly from stop to stop — feel free to swap the order around depending on where you're starting from.

items.activity: Start at Wat Chaiyo Worawihan in Chaiyo district to pay respects to Luang Pho To in the tall viharn
items.note: Coming early means nice light and fewer people

items.activity: Move on to Wat Ton Son in Ang Thong town to pay respects to Somdej Phra Si Mueang Thong
items.note: It's in town, so parking and coffee shops are easy to find

items.activity: Head to Wat Khun Inthapramun in Pho Thong district for the long reclining Buddha out in the fields
items.note: Wide open plaza — bring an umbrella and a sun hat

items.activity: Break for lunch at a local spot, such as boat noodles or a riverside restaurant
items.note: See our Ang Thong food guide for ideas

items.activity: Finish at Wat Pa Mok Worawihan in Pa Mok district for the old reclining Buddha
items.note: Stop by the nearby Bang Sadet court-doll village while you're there

items.activity: Drop by the Ekkarat drum-making village or pick up souvenirs before heading back
items.note: If you have time left, add Wat Muang as one more stop

blocks.title: Travel tips
blocks.html: Driving yourself is by far the easiest, since the temples are spread across several districts and public transport between them is scarce. Coming from Bangkok, take the Asia Highway (Route 32) then branch off into Ang Thong town — the whole trip is about 1.5–2 hours.

faq.q: Which Ang Thong temples are must-sees?
faq.a: If you're short on time, go for the four main temples: Wat Khun Inthapramun (the long reclining Buddha), Wat Pa Mok Worawihan (the old reclining Buddha), Wat Chaiyo Worawihan (Luang Pho To) and Wat Ton Son (the town temple). All four are close together and can be visited back-to-back in a single day.

faq.q: How long is the reclining Buddha at Wat Khun Inthapramun?
faq.a: The figure is around 50 metres long, one of the longest reclining Buddhas in Thailand. It sits in the open in the Pho Thong fields and is thought to date back to the Sukhothai period, with restorations across several eras since.

faq.q: Is one day enough for Ang Thong's temples?
faq.a: Yes. The main temples are about 20–30 minutes apart by car, so if you start in the morning and drive yourself, you can comfortably visit four or five temples, stop for lunch and pick up souvenirs all in one day.

faq.q: Are Ang Thong's temples free, and how should I dress?
faq.a: Most temples are free, with donations welcome. Dress modestly — no sleeveless tops or shorts when entering the viharn, especially at royal temples like Wat Pa Mok and Wat Chaiyo.

faq.q: What time do Ang Thong's temples open?
faq.a: Most temples are open for worship daily, roughly 08:00–17:00. Hours can shift around merit festivals or the season, so it's best to go from morning to early afternoon to leave time to visit several temples in a row.
